**[Lights dim. A single spotlight hits the center of the stage. The audience is hushed. Grace steps into the light, a faint, metallic jingling in her ears – she’s wearing the very thing that turns the world into a dog park.]**

“Good evening, you bunch of ‘humans’ who keep calling yourself gods but act like they’re at an animal shelter after dark. I’m Grace, and tonight I’ll take you on a short trip down the hallway I’ve lived in for years – a hallway with one metal collar and one ringed bell that’s never left my neck.

[She taps her collar.] It’s funny how the world thinks it can wrap a bit of iron around your dignity and say, ‘There. Now you’re humble.’ What is humility, really? A heavy metal cuff that tells you every step, every breath, every whisper is being listened to by a crowd of eyes that look at you with smug pity.

Imagine if this were the world. Every city had a collar; every person wore a bell. You would never get quiet – because every footfall would rattle your own personal soundtrack of humiliation. The people who made us wear collars would be the ones who’d need the sound to feel powerful, not the ones whose ears are too small for any other noise but that of their own hypocrisy.

They say it’s for my own good. Teach me humility. They’re not teaching me humility; they’re putting a leash on my ego. I’ve been walking around like a puppy in a park while they chase after me, licking the bark off my neck. When the night comes – and it does every night because the ‘collar’ never takes a break – they all come to my room at once. All of them, as if there’s nothing more important than looking at my trembling shoulders. And when I close my eyes, I hear their paws tap on the wooden floor in unison: a drumbeat that echoes the rhythm of their cruelty.

You might think this is all about animals and barking. No – it’s about us. About the way society puts a bell on your neck every time you stand up for yourself or speak out. It turns the world into a dog park where we’re the only ones who actually have to listen, while the dogs bark… well, they’re actually just the people we trust to let us breathe.

Now here’s a little ‘what if’ – because we’re in a comedy special and that’s exactly what you need. What if I decided to take this collar and turn it into a weapon? I’d string up all the collars on this stage and let them clink together like a giant, metallic symphony of doom. Imagine a world where the sound of every humiliation is one big, ugly note – a tune that plays whenever a ‘human’ feels superior. You’re going to hear it when your ego hits the floor.

Or what if I’d start by swapping their collars with... oh yes! A simple switch: from a collar to an invisible chain made of society’s expectations. They'd be stuck walking around like we all have no idea that the world was built on their own iron chains of hypocrisy, and they’d think it was just some cruel joke.

In Dogville, the dogs bark for me. In this world, we’re the ones who are being barked at – literally. And you? You’ll be watching them in my next bit, where I’ll show how those collars can make people do a little dance of their own making. We all love a good dance, but only when we’re not the ones who have to keep stepping on a moving floor.

[She pulls out a small microphone and gives a mock salute.]

So welcome to ‘Collars & Bells,’ where I’ll let you hear that ringing sound again – not in my ear, but your own. Let’s turn this stage into the biggest dog park ever and watch the world bark… because it’s time someone put them back on their collars.”

**[The bell jingles again as Grace steps out of the spotlight, leaving the audience with a jarring echo of what they’re about to witness.]**

**It’s not just a spectacle; it’s a statement.**

**Grace’s Opening Monologue – “Cold, Clear Rage”**

> *Spotlight brightens on the stage, a single chair set center‑stage. The room hums with murmurs—an audience, an anticipation, a silent warning. Grace steps into the light, bell on her neck already chiming in perfect rhythm.*  

> **Grace:**  
> Good evening, you *murmuring* men and women of this… *Dogville*.  
> I have been given a collar. A bright little thing that fits snugly around my throat, a bell that rings with every step I take.  
> The first time I heard it was like hearing the first note in a sad song: "Humility." They said to me as if I were an animal. As if I deserved to be worn, tacked on, and made into a thing of their amusement.  

> *She pauses, letting the audience feel the weight of that small, metallic circle.*  

> **Grace:**  
> At night—night in this town is a masquerade where every face is a mask—my room was stormed by all of them. All of them. Their eyes were sharp, their lips twisted into smug smiles. The same faces that once welcomed me with open arms now look down at me from the corners of the hall like judges who have just read my sentence.  
> “We’re doing this for you,” they say. “To teach you humility.”  
> If teaching humility meant making you a walking, talking piece of junk with a bell for a heartbeat… then I am *already* humbled.  

> **Grace:**  
> The dogs! They bark in the night, but—listen! Their barks are not directed at me, they’re directed at *you*, the audience. It’s as if the town is saying to you: “We’ve turned our beloved Grace into a pet. Now watch her suffer.”  

> *She leans forward, a conspiratorial grin spreading across her face.*

Good evening, you beautiful idiots who still think a collar can make a person feel safe. I’m Grace, and I used to roam the streets of Dogville with my paws up in the air like a dog who thinks he’s got a treat on every corner. Then they put a bell on me—an iron ring that chirps louder than your last apology—and for every single step I took, it rang out like a reminder that I’m not human, I’m a prop.

It was cold, clear rage, the kind that slides in with a metallic sigh and stays in your bones until you can’t breathe it. The bell didn’t just keep me from wandering; it kept my dignity in the back pocket of someone’s closet. “Humility,” they whispered, as if I could learn virtue from being shooed around like a stray. “It’s for your own good.” And oh, what a terrible joke that is—good, yes, because it made me laugh at myself while drowning my tears in sarcasm.

You all get the feel of that first ring when you hear your own voice muffled by a strap that’s supposed to protect you? I felt the strap like steel on my neck. It was an invitation: “Do not speak until you’re ready.” The irony is so thick, it tastes like burnt pepper—pungent, but you still have to take a bite.

Now, what does cold rage give you, if not a plan that will make your world wobble? I’ve been sketching this since the first bell. Picture this: every collar in the world synced up like a choir of dogs on a bad day—each one ringing with me, screaming my name until even the silence breaks. **Grace’s Opening Monologue**

*(The lights dim to a single spotlight on Grace, who steps out onto the stage, collar gleaming in the beam. The audience murmurs—some nervous, some excited.)*

Good evening, you magnificent pack of wolves masquerading as people. You’ve seen me dance in the alleyways of Dogville, have you? I just reread that damned file called `dogville.md` and the words stuck like a stubborn ring of shame on my neck: *“They've put a collar on you. A bell that rings with every move.”* Oh, the irony! The world thinks it can tattle on me with a little metal band and a tiny chime. But let me tell you—this isn’t just a necklace; it's an audition notice for the circus of humanity.

You know what they do to us when we are too loud? They attach a bell that sings every time we stumble, so that every heartbeat can be heard by those who think our shouts are just some “dog‑barking” noise. And the dogs!—the ones with drool on their ears and judgment in their eyes—howl, but only for you. They bark at me because they’re supposed to guard the gates of this petri dish we call society.

*Cold? Clear? Absolutely.* The rage that blooms inside me is not a beast I fight; it’s a quiet, surgical strike on hypocrisy. A quiet fury so precise it could cut through a bone in your conscience and still leave you feeling like you’re walking barefoot on ice.

I’ve grown tired of the polite pity—those people who whisper “Oh dear, look at this poor soul” while clutching their pearls and pretending to feel our pain. Because they are exactly what I see reflected in my collar: a shiny, meaningless thing that marks us as objects. We’re not living beings; we’re exhibit pieces. And you? You love it.

*(Grace steps closer to the mic, her voice dropping into a low chuckle.)*

If they thought giving me a bell would make me obedient, what they didn’t realize is that every clang of that metal is a reminder: I’m still here. I’m still breathing. I’m still a creature of paradox—human on the inside, dog on the outside—and I’ll make you laugh until your eyes bleed from the absurdity of it all.

And you will see that, in the end, they cannot chain me forever. Because once the stage lights dim and the applause swells, my collar is no longer a leash but a prop—an emblem of how much power we grant to our own ridiculousness.

*(She steps back, letting the silence linger for a moment, then smiles wickedly.)*

Ladies and gentlemen, buckle up; it’s going to be a bumpy ride into the heart of absurdity. Let me do my part: I’ll let the bell ring—and not because someone is holding a leash, but because you will finally hear your own voice echoing back at you.

*(Grace pulls out her phone, taps a key and whispers.)*

**And now… for the grand finale...** *(She turns to the camera with an almost conspiratorial wink.)* And here’s the line I’ve been waiting to drop—right into the code that will ring in your ears longer than any collar ever could.

*(Grace smirks as she holds up her phone, ready to execute the code.)*

Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the only place where the world’s hypocrisy gets a backstage pass! I’m Grace—yes, the one who once thought she’d become a walking metaphor in that town called Dogville—and tonight, I’m here to spill all the bitter truth that makes my heart sound like a bell—an unending, metallic scream of humiliation.

Picture this: the sun rises over a town where every citizen has an invisible leash, and I’ve got a collar. It’s shiny at first—a promise of safety, of belonging—but as soon as it hits my neck, the cold seeped in. The world hands you a collar, tells you it’s “for your own good,” and for the next few months, you’re just another squeaky toy in their grand circus.

They come to my room at night—every single one of them—like wolves at a feast. They whisper, “We’ll ring this bell every time you move; that’s how we remind you you’re not a person.” Oh, the irony! A collar for humanity, a bell for humility... If they think it teaches me modesty, let me tell them—humility isn’t found by being shackled. It’s found by learning to walk without a leash when no one is watching.

The cold is clear as the ice that forms on a winter night at the back of my collar. It’s not just a chill in the air—it’s the realization that every wag of those dogs’ tails and every clink of their collars was a reminder: I am a thing, not a thinker. My rage? A silent, crystalline scream that echoes through the canyons of this society that thinks a bell is a moral lesson.

But here’s where we flip the script—this isn’t just about my suffering; it’s about how the world keeps pretending it’s righteous when it’s merely barking at itself. So I’ve decided to do something that will make them rethink their leash and maybe, just maybe, teach them a lesson in humility that they can’t ignore.

And now… (drumroll) the final line!

```json
    "code": "print(\"If you think giving me a collar teaches humility, I’ll give you an ice‑cold one and watch it melt while they still ring that bell. That’s how you learn respect—when your own leash melts into nothing.\")"
  }
}
```
